candidate_findings.message: This change connects `updateItem` to the UI, but `updateItem` never records an activity. Adding an item logs 'added' and deleting logs 'removed', yet editing an item (name, SKU, quantity, price) leaves nothing in Recent Activity. `ActivityEntry['action']` already includes 'updated', and the mock data uses it, so the gap is easy to notice. If the goal is complete CRUD, the update path should log an 'updated' (or 'restocked') activity like the other two operations do, and a test should cover it.

The new test calls `renderHook` without StrictMode, so it misses a real bug. `deleteItem` calls `setActivities` from inside the `setItems` updater, and updaters must be pure. `main.tsx` wraps the app in `<StrictMode>`, which runs updaters twice in development, so each delete in dev adds two 'removed' activities. The test passes only because it does not render the way the app does. Move the activity creation out of the updater (look up the item from current `items` first, or use a reducer), and run the test with `{ wrapper: StrictMode }` so it catches this.

When `editItem` is set but `onUpdate` is missing (it is optional in the props), the code falls through to `onAdd(form)`. An attempted edit then silently creates a duplicate item, and the modal still shows 'Edit Item' / 'Save Changes'. Edit mode should require `onUpdate`, either through the prop types (a discriminated union) or with an explicit guard, rather than quietly adding a new item.

Edit mode always sends the whole form to `onUpdate`, even when nothing changed. So clicking Edit and then 'Save Changes' without touching anything still bumps `lastUpdated`. Edits also skip any check for duplicate SKUs. Consider sending only the changed fields, or skipping the update when nothing changed.

None of the new UI behaviour has tests: the Edit button, the modal pre-filling in edit mode, the form resetting after cancel/reopen, and `onUpdate` being called with the item's id. Those are the main claims of this PR, but the only test added covers delete activity. Add component tests for the edit flow and for the form reset.

Saving an edit calls `updateItem`, which changes the item but never adds an activity entry. `ActivityEntry['action']` already includes `'updated'`, and `RecentActivity` has a config for it, but nothing ever emits it. As a result, edits (including quantity changes that move an item between In Stock, Low Stock and Out of Stock) never appear in the dashboard's Recent Activity feed, while adds and deletes do. Now that edits are reachable from the UI, `updateItem` should log an `'updated'` activity the same way `addItem` and `deleteItem` do.

This test locks in a buggy implementation. `deleteItem` calls `setActivities` from inside the `setItems` updater function, which is a side effect inside a function that should be pure. The app runs under `<StrictMode>` (`src/main.tsx`), and in development StrictMode calls updater functions twice, so one delete logs two 'removed' activities. `renderHook` runs without StrictMode here, so the `+1` assertion passes and hides the problem. Fix `deleteItem` first: look up the item outside the updater, then call `setItems` and `setActivities` separately. Consider also running this test with a StrictMode wrapper.

If the modal gets `editItem` but no `onUpdate`, it falls through to `onAdd(form)`. Saving an edit would then silently create a duplicate item instead of updating the original. Since `onUpdate` is optional in the props, this misuse is easy to hit. Either make edit mode require `onUpdate` (for example, a discriminated union in the props type) or skip the add branch when `editItem` is set.

None of the new edit behaviour has tests. Nothing covers the Edit button, the pre-filled form, the 'Save Changes' path calling `onUpdate`, or the form resetting when the modal is reopened via the `modalKey` remount. These were the main goals of the PR, but only the delete-activity test was added. A component test for edit-and-save and for cancel-then-reopen would catch regressions here.

Default the new optional repository list to an empty array. For existing deployments with a customized `config.yaml` that lacks `ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS`, this validation rejects an otherwise valid configuration. The catch handler then discards all configured settings, including `ORGANIZATION_NAME`, causing the catalog to request unfiltered Hugging Face listings and lose its branding. Default an absent field to `[]` in both the frontend and export script, while continuing to reject explicitly malformed values.

The PR description says ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS is optional and defaults to [] when absent, but the code requires it. If the key is missing, or a single entry is malformed, validation throws and the whole config falls back to defaults, including ORGANIZATION_NAME: ''. The page then shows a configuration error and an empty catalog (main.js:897 returns early). Any existing catalog whose config.yaml predates this key breaks after this change. Either treat a missing key as [] (e.g. `CONFIG.ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS ??= []`), or update the PR description and announce it as a breaking change. Also consider skipping bad entries with a warning instead of discarding the entire valid config.

Same mismatch as main.js: the script throws if ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS is absent, even though the feature is described as optional with a default of []. The key also isn't in `requiredKeys`, and the header comment (lines 11-12) doesn't mention it, so required-key handling is inconsistent within this script.

Validation only checks `e.repo.trim()`. The untrimmed `entry.repo` is still used for deduplication and in the fetch URL, so a value with stray whitespace passes validation but requests a bad URL (fails silently with a warning) and isn't matched against existing org IDs. Dedup is also case-sensitive even though Hub IDs are case-insensitive. Entries like `User/Repo` and `user/repo` are both fetched, return the same canonical `item.id`, and both get added because the final filter only checks `existingIds`, not IDs already fetched. The result is duplicate cards. Normalize (trim, lowercase) before dedup, and dedup the fetched results by `item.id`.
Same normalization/dedup gap as main.js: `entry.repo` is used untrimmed, and the fetched items aren't deduplicated by their returned `id`.

For `models`, each additional repo is fetched from `${API_BASE_URL}models/${repo}`, then fetched again from the same endpoint in the Step 2 detail loop. That doubles the requests per additional model. Skip the detail fetch for items that already came from the per-repo endpoint.

The PR description says ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS is optional and defaults to [] when absent, but the code requires it. Any existing config.yaml without this key now fails validation. That throws, shows the 'Configuration Error' banner, and replaces the whole CONFIG with the hard-coded defaults (ORGANIZATION_NAME ''). The catalog then renders nothing, even though the rest of the config is valid. Either default a missing key to [] (e.g. `CONFIG.ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS ??= []`) or correct the description and flag this as a breaking config change.

One malformed ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS entry (a typo like `type: dataset` or a missing `repo`) sends the whole config to the defaults fallback, which wipes ORGANIZATION_NAME, colors, title and so on. A small mistake in an optional extra list takes down the entire catalog. A better fix is to warn and skip just the bad entries, the way a failed per-repo fetch is handled.

The tag export script also throws when ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS is absent. That contradicts the 'optional, defaults to []' behavior in the description and breaks the script for existing configs. ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS also isn't added to `requiredKeys` or to the header comment (lines 11-12) that lists which config keys the script reads, so the behavior is inconsistent and undocumented.

Validation calls `e.repo.trim()` to reject blank strings, but the untrimmed `entry.repo` is what goes into the dedupe check and the fetch URL. An entry like `" user/name"` or `"user/name "` passes validation, then 404s or fails dedupe. The repo format (owner/name) isn't validated either, so a pasted full URL is accepted and fails silently with only a console warning. Normalize (trim) the value when assigning ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS, and check the `owner/name` shape.

Dedupe compares exact `entry.repo` strings, but HF repo IDs are case-insensitive. Two config entries that differ only in case (e.g. `User/Repo` and `user/repo`) both get fetched, and both survive the final `!existingIds.has(item.id)` filter, because that filter only checks org items and not other fetched items. The same repo then shows up twice. Dedupe fetched results by their returned `item.id` (or compare lowercased IDs).

For `models`, each additional repo is fetched from `${API_BASE_URL}models/${repo}` here, then fetched again from the same detail endpoint in Step 2 (line 332). That doubles requests to the HF API, which matters for rate limits as the list grows. The same duplication exists in scripts/export-tags.js (lines 132-150). Skip the pre-fetch for models, or skip the Step 2 detail fetch for items that already came from the detail endpoint.

Additional HF repos that fail to fetch are dropped silently (`.catch(() => null)`) with no log. The browser code warns on these failures, but here a typo'd repo just makes its tags disappear from tag-export.txt, and the summary count is the only clue. Log a warning like main.js does.

This PR takes `defmt` out of the default features, and nothing about PartitionGuard needs that. It is a breaking change for downstream crates: anyone relying on the default `Error: defmt::Format` derive will stop compiling unless they turn the feature back on themselves. If tests needed this, enable or disable `defmt` only in the test or CI configuration. Otherwise, revert it, or at least call it out as breaking in the PR and changelog.

The new dev-dependency `critical-section` (with `std`) is not used by any test code. All tests use `NoopRawMutex`, and nothing references critical_section. It looks like a leftover from working around the defmt/link problem. Remove it, or explain why it is needed.

`Partition::lock`/`try_lock` lock the single Mutex shared by every partition of the device, not just this partition. While a PartitionGuard is alive, all other partitions are blocked too (the test even relies on this: holding `factory.lock()` makes `settings.try_lock()` fail). This makes it easy to deadlock: if a task holds a guard and then awaits any other `Partition` method, or `lock()`, on the same device, it waits forever. The docs ('exclusive access to a partition's underlying storage') hide this. State clearly that the guard locks the whole device and must not be held across other partition accesses.

This only partly delivers what the motivation promises. `try_lock` is synchronous, but every operation on the guard (BlockDevice/NorFlash read/write/erase) is async. A synchronous panic handler would still need its own executor or `block_on` to use it. Also, if the panicking task held the lock, `try_lock` just fails, so crash data still cannot be written in exactly the case described. Consider documenting the intended usage, or offering a blocking path.

There is no way to turn a `PartitionGuard<RW>` into an RO view, the way `Partition::readonly()` does for partitions. As a result, the RW guard impls duplicate the read logic instead of delegating to it (see bdd.rs).

`start_block` and `check_access` (and `within_bounds` in lib.rs) are copied verbatim from `Partition` into `PartitionGuard`, and the BlockDevice read/write bodies are duplicated again for RO and RW guards. Any future fix to the bounds or overflow logic has to be made in several places, which invites drift in security-relevant checks. Move this into a shared helper, for example a function over `(offset, size)` or a small shared bounds struct.

This changes behavior silently. Before, `erase(from, to)` with `to < from` used `saturating_sub`, so the request was passed to the device, which would report its own error. Now it returns `Error::OutOfBounds`, which maps to NorFlashErrorKind::OutOfBounds. That is reasonable, but it changes the error kind callers see, and no test or PR note covers it.

`defmt` was removed from the default features, and the PR description doesn't mention it. Downstream crates that use the defaults and depend on `Error<E>: defmt::Format` (or log it with defmt) will stop compiling. This is a breaking API change unrelated to PartitionGuard. Revert it, or call it out and handle it as a semver-breaking change.

`lock()`/`try_lock()` lock the mutex for the whole storage device, not just this partition. While a PartitionGuard is alive, every other partition (and the same `Partition` through its own trait methods, which call `self.storage.lock().await`) waits forever if used in the same task. That is an easy self-deadlock to hit, e.g. `let g = p.lock().await; p.read(..).await`. None of this is documented: the doc comments suggest the guard is per-partition. State clearly that the guard locks the whole device and that the partition (and its siblings) must not be used while it is held.

The motivation is to let panic handlers reach storage. But every PartitionGuard operation is `async`, so a synchronous panic handler still needs an executor or `block_on` to use it. Also, if the panicking task held the lock in the middle of a flash operation, `try_lock` fails and the data can't be written anyway. The use case is only partly solved and this isn't documented. Consider documenting the limits, or offering a way to recover or force access.

`start_block` and `check_access` are copied word for word from the `Partition` impl, `within_bounds` is copied in lib.rs (lines 138-148), and the BlockDevice/NorFlash bodies are repeated too. Later fixes to the bounds logic can easily land in one copy and not the other. Move the shared logic into a helper that works on `(offset, size)`, and have both `Partition` and `PartitionGuard` call it.

Behaviour change: `erase(from, to)` with `from > to` used to pass `saturating_sub` = 0 through the bounds check and let the underlying driver report its own error (usually NotAligned or another driver-specific error). It now returns `Error::OutOfBounds`. That may be fine, but it is a silent semantic change to the existing `Partition` API, and the PR doesn't mention or test it.

`#[allow(unused)]` on the public `PartitionGuard` struct (and on its `within_bounds`) hides real dead-code warnings when the `esa`/`bdd` features are off. In that case the guard has no usable methods at all. Gate the guard with `cfg` on those features, or drop the blanket allow.

`Partition<RW>` has `readonly()` to downgrade to RO, but `PartitionGuard<RW>` has no equivalent. So a write-capable guard can't be handed to code that expects a read-only one, and the API is inconsistent. Consider adding `PartitionGuard::readonly`.

Verify the approval hash before retrying a push. If the plan file changes after its original approval, `--push` now publishes the modified file while preserving a marker that approves different bytes. Before falling through to Step 4c, compare the current plan hash with the existing marker and require re-approval on mismatch or a malformed marker.

Accept Notion page IDs in bracketed Source values. A Notion brief's Source contains a bracketed page ID, but this parser accepts only numeric or project-number keys. Consequently, valid Notion Sources are classified as file paths and skipped, even with `--push`; the later Notion validation and transport are unreachable without an explicit override. Extract bracketed keys broadly enough to include Notion UUIDs, then apply the configured board's validation.

Check Linear mutation results before logging push success. Linear can return HTTP 200 with GraphQL `errors` or an unsuccessful `commentCreate` result. Treating every 2xx response as a live comment records `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH` despite no publication and omits the failure message and retry command. Check the GraphQL response body and require `data.commentCreate.success` before taking this success branch.

`--ticket` can't actually override a missing or non-bracketed Source. Step 4c checks for a missing `**Source:**` header and skips silently, and it sends inline-quoted or file-path Sources to BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET. Both checks run before `--ticket` is looked at. The command docs and line 394 say `--ticket` is for when the Source field is "missing, ambiguous" and that the retry path works if "`--ticket` override must be supplied". With the steps in this order, `/clancy:approve-plan stem --push --ticket PROJ-1` on a plan with no Source, or a quoted or file Source, never pushes. Resolve `--ticket` first and parse Source only when no override is given.

The bracketed-key regex `^\[(#?\d+|[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*-\d+)\]` can't match a Notion page ID (32/36 hex characters). It also rejects lowercase keys and Shortcut-style `SC-123`. Brief writes Notion tickets as `[{KEY}] Title`, so a Notion Source falls into the catch-all and gets logged as `file-path`. That means Notion auto-detect can never push, yet the workflow still ships a Notion curl block and a Notion-only success note. The audit token also records the wrong reason. Make the bracket pattern generic (e.g. `^\[([^\]]+)\]\s+.+$`) and let the per-board validation decide.

The EEXIST + `--push` retry path doesn't check that the plan file still matches the marker's `sha256=` before pushing. If someone edits the plan after approval, the retry posts the edited, unapproved content to the board as the "approved plan". The marker stays as it was, so the plan inventory would show it as Stale. Before falling through to Step 4c, hash the plan again and compare it to the marker. On mismatch, refuse to push and tell the user to re-approve.

This line says the retry "preserves the original approval timestamp — auditing tools see one approval row". But Step 4c always continues to Step 7, and Step 7's local-mode block always appends `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN` and prints "✅ Approved {stem}". Each retry therefore writes another approval row and shows a fresh approval message. Step 4 (Confirm) also asks "Approve this plan? [Y/n]" again before 4a gets to the EEXIST check. Step 7 (and Step 4) need a retry branch that skips the approval row and message.

Step 2 still says "The board push offer for plan-file-stem mode is deferred to a future PR — for now the local marker is the only side effect." That now contradicts Step 4c. An LLM following the workflow in order may never run the push. This stale line was missed when the other PR-reference prose was removed.

Key validation and the mismatch hard-error come before the decision matrix. Under `--afk` without `--push`, the matrix says no push happens and only LOCAL_ONLY is logged. But an auto-detected Source key that fails the board regex will already have printed a hard error, logged `BOARD_PUSH_FAILED | key-mismatch`, and shown a retry command, even though no push was intended. The same happens when an interactive user would have answered No. Apply the matrix's --afk/--push gate before validating.

The failure handling relies on the HTTP status ("When the curl returns a 2xx", "Use the literal numeric status code"). The duplicated curl blocks use plain `curl -s` with no `-w '%{http_code}'` or `--fail`, so curl exits 0 on 4xx/5xx and the status is never captured. Nothing tells the agent how to map curl exit codes to `dns`/`timeout`/`network`. As written, a 403/404 will probably be treated as success and logged as LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH. Add explicit status capture outside the duplicated region.

The duplicated curl blocks use `$TICKET_KEY`, `$ISSUE_NUMBER`, `$ISSUE_ID`, `$WORK_ITEM_ID`, `$STORY_ID` and `$PAGE_ID`. In plan.md these are set by earlier steps; Step 4c never says how to get them from `{KEY}`. Examples: strip `#` for GitHub, and resolve the Linear identifier (ENG-42) to the issue UUID the way Step 3 does. Step 4c also never defines the comment payload. Locked decision 4 says "full plan content + one-line approval header", but no header text or format is given, so pushes will be inconsistent or fail (Linear in particular).

The ordering of progress rows can't be followed. The skip row (and the success row at line 742) must be appended "after the existing LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN row from Step 7", but Step 4c runs before Step 7, so that row doesn't exist yet. Either have Step 4c defer its row to Step 7 or drop the ordering claim. Both references also use the old `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN | {stem}` / `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN | sha256=` column order that the M1 fix meant to remove (the actual row is `{stem} | LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN | sha256=`).

The Step 4c per-board regexes disagree with Step 2's ticket-key validation for the same board. Step 2 is case-insensitive, allows a bare number for GitHub, allows `SC-123` for Shortcut, and allows `notion-[a-f0-9]{8}` for Notion. A key that Step 2 accepts as a valid ticket argument can be rejected by Step 4c's `--ticket` validation.

Nothing says what happens when the interactive user answers N at the `[y/N]` push prompt. There's no routing statement and no progress token, unlike the `--afk`-without-`--push` cell, which logs LOCAL_ONLY. The audit trail can't tell a declined push from a run where the gate was never reached.

Several new tests slice by `indexOf`/`search` without asserting the index is found. Examples: the 4a→4c span, `skipRegion`, `failRegion`, `mismatchRegion`, `localOnlyRegion`. If a heading or token is renamed, `indexOf` returns -1. The span then becomes empty or a single trailing character, and the negative `not.toMatch` assertions pass without checking anything. This is the same blind spot that hid H2. Assert `> -1` before slicing.

The EEXIST + `--push` retry path never re-hashes the plan file or compares it to the marker's `sha256=`. If the plan was edited after approval, a retry posts the edited, unapproved content to the board as the 'approved plan', while the local marker says it is stale. The retry should verify the current hash matches the marker and refuse on mismatch (point the user to delete and re-approve).

The retry contract says 'auditing tools see one approval row… even if 4c was attempted multiple times'. But the retry still goes through Step 7's local-mode block, which always prints '✅ Approved {stem}' and always appends another `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN | sha256=…` row (line ~1515). Nothing tells Step 7 to suppress the approval row or banner on a retry, so every retry adds a duplicate approval row and falsely re-announces approval. Step 4 ('Approve this plan? [Y/n]') also prompts again for a plan that is already approved.

There is no idempotency check on `EEXIST + --push`. If the earlier push succeeded (a `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH` row exists for this stem) or the user just re-runs with `--push`, the full plan is posted to the ticket a second time. The step only says 'retry a previously failed push' and never checks progress.txt for a prior success.

Stale prose not updated by this PR: Step 2 still says 'The board push offer for plan-file-stem mode is deferred to a future PR — for now the local marker is the only side effect.' That contradicts the new Step 4c. An LLM following the workflow in order will read this first. The PR's own H2/L2 fix only scanned 4a→4c, so this was missed.

`--ticket` cannot do what it is documented for. The missing-Source branch skips Step 4c silently, and the inline-quoted/file-path branch logs BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET, both before the override is ever consulted. Yet `--ticket` is documented as the fix for when 'the brief Source field is missing' and as the retry key. So `--push --ticket KEY` on a plan whose Source is missing or non-bracketed never pushes. On top of that, an explicit `--push` that ends in a silent skip gives the user no feedback. The `--ticket` override needs to be resolved before Source parsing and the skip branches.

The bracketed-key classifier `^\[(#?\d+|[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*-\d+)\]` only accepts numeric or uppercase-PREFIX-digits keys. Notion keys are 32/36-char lowercase hex (and the Step 2 `notion-xxxxxxxx` short form), so a Notion Source like `[abc123…] Title` falls into the 'file path' bucket and is logged as `BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET | file-path`. Auto-detect therefore never pushes on Notion, even though the six-platform table and the Notion-only Step 7 note assume it does. Lowercase Jira/Linear keys and Shortcut `SC-123` keys are rejected the same way.

The per-platform regexes contradict Step 2's ticket validation in the same file. Step 2 is case-insensitive, accepts a bare number for GitHub, `SC-123` for Shortcut, `notion-[a-f0-9]{8}` for Notion, and `[A-Za-z]{1,10}` prefixes for Linear. Step 4c uses case-sensitive anchored patterns that reject all of these. A key that approve-plan accepts in board mode can hard-error as a 'mismatch' in 4c (e.g. `--ticket 42` on GitHub, `--ticket eng-42` on Linear). Also, the Notion alternative `^[0-9a-f-]{36}$` accepts any 36-char string of hex and dashes, e.g. 36 dashes.

The duplicated curl blocks use `$TICKET_KEY`, `$ISSUE_NUMBER`, `$ISSUE_ID`, `$WORK_ITEM_ID`, `$STORY_ID`, `$PAGE_ID`, but Step 4c never says how to derive them from the validated `{KEY}`. For example, GitHub needs the `#` stripped, and Linear's `issueId` / Notion's `page_id` may need ID resolution. In `plan.md` these variables come from the ticket-fetch context that 4c does not have. Without a mapping step, the push is underspecified and likely to hit the wrong endpoint (e.g. `/issues/#50/comments`).

Success and failure are classified by HTTP status ('2xx', literal non-2xx code), but every curl block is `curl -s` with no `-w '%{http_code}'`/`-f`, so the status code is never captured. Linear's GraphQL API also returns HTTP 200 with an `errors` array or `success: false` when it fails. As written, Linear failures will be logged as `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH` successes. The `auth` error class ('credential-rejection signal that isn't a clean HTTP status') is also undefined at the transport layer.

Locked spec decision 4 ('full plan content + one-line approval header') is not implemented anywhere in Step 4c. The step never says what the comment body is or what the approval header line looks like; the only payload hints are the `<markdown plan>` placeholders in the copied blocks. Implementations will diverge, and the comment won't show that it is an approved plan rather than a draft.

Pushing the full local plan file posts a comment that contains the `## Clancy Implementation Plan` heading. The board flow treats that heading as the marker for a plan comment (Step 3 picks 'the most recent comment body containing' it, and `/clancy:plan` uses it to detect existing plans). A later `/clancy:approve-plan KEY` or `/clancy:plan KEY` on that ticket will treat the pushed approval comment as the pending plan to promote or revise. Either strip/rename the heading or document the interaction.

The row ordering is impossible as written. Step 4c's tokens (BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET, LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH, BOARD_PUSH_FAILED, LOCAL_ONLY) are said to be written 'after the existing LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN row from Step 7's log block', but Step 7 runs after Step 4c. Either Step 4c must buffer its rows until Step 7, or the rows land before the approval row. The workflow should say which.

Validation and the hard error (with a `BOARD_PUSH_FAILED | key-mismatch` row) are specified before the decision matrix and apply unconditionally. In the `--afk` without `--push` cell, and when the user would answer N, an auto-detected key that doesn't match still produces a hard error and a failure row, even though no push was ever going to happen. Step 4c also never says what to log or print when the user declines the `[y/N]` prompt.

The 'validates BEFORE any push attempt' test uses `fourCBody.search(/validat/i)`. That matches the first occurrence of 'validat' anywhere in Step 4c (e.g. the 'same gate evaluation' or flag prose), so it passes whatever order the validation section is in. Like the other prose-regex tests here, it gives weak protection against regressions.

This migration is described as only adding the `data` column, but it also changes the primary key of all three tables (`ratelimitconfig`, `ratelimitcounter`, `ratelimitentry`) from AutoField to BigAutoField. On PostgreSQL and MySQL that rewrites each table and holds an exclusive lock for the whole rewrite. Rate-limit tables are hit on every request and can be large, so `migrate` can cause downtime or block traffic for a long time. Neither the CHANGELOG nor the upgrade notes mention it. Put the PK change in its own documented migration, or leave it out of this bug-fix release. The `data` AddField alone is enough to fix #24.

Whether the RenameIndex operations are included depends on which Django version runs the migration. The project still supports Django 3.2 and 4.0, which have no RenameIndex. On those versions the migration state keeps the old index names while the models expect the new ones. That leaves pending autodetected changes (`makemigrations --check` fails), and any later migration that refers to the new index names will break on those installs. A migration's operations should be the same on every version. Drop the cosmetic renames, or do them with a version-independent approach such as RemoveIndex/AddIndex, or with SeparateDatabaseAndState plus RunSQL.

A personal working checklist is committed to the repository root. It includes the author's local absolute paths (`/Users/<author>/...`). It is not project documentation and should be removed from the change.

"apply the latest migration before upgrading" can't be followed, because the migration only arrives with the upgrade. It should say to run `migrate` after upgrading, before serving traffic. The entry also leaves out the BigAutoField PK changes and index renames included in the same migration.

`get()` now returns the JSON-decoded `data` whenever it is set, not `counter.count`. Values written through `set()` are first converted with `str()`, so their types change on the way back: `set(k, "123")` returns `get(k) == 123`, and `set(k, "true")` returns `True`. Token-bucket keys now return a dict instead of an int. Callers that relied on `get()` returning the count may break. Store values in a typed JSON envelope, or document the new behavior.

This bug fix has no regression tests. The PR's "I have added tests" box is unchecked, even though the committed checklist marks tests as added. Nothing tests that token-bucket state (fractional tokens, last_refill) persists across calls, that rows with `data` NULL from before the migration fall back correctly, or what `get()` now returns. Because `token_bucket_check` fails open on any exception, a regression here would quietly turn off rate limiting.

This bug-fix migration also changes the primary keys of all three tables from AutoField to BigAutoField. 0001_initial created them as AutoField. On PostgreSQL and MySQL this rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock, and RateLimitEntry and RateLimitCounter can be large, busy tables. The PR describes only 'adding the data column' and claims backwards compatibility, so this downtime risk is unannounced. Split the PK change into its own documented migration, or leave it out of this patch.

Which operations run depends on the installed Django version. On Django 3.2 and 4.0, which pyproject still supports, the RenameIndex operations are skipped. The migration state then keeps the old index names, but the model Meta auto-generates the new ones. On those versions `migrate` warns about unreflected model changes, `makemigrations --check` fails in user projects, and running makemigrations creates a stray migration inside the installed package. The DB schema also differs between Django versions. Use version-independent operations (e.g. RunSQL/SeparateDatabaseAndState), or give the model indexes explicit names that match 0001.

If the new migration hasn't been applied, every token_bucket_check fails on the missing `data` column. The broad `except Exception` turns that into 'allow the request', so rate limiting is silently off with only an error log. The upgrade now depends on a migration, so this fail-open path deserves a louder signal (e.g. a system check for the column) rather than just README notes.

get() now returns deserialize_data(counter.data) without an expected type. Because set() stores scalars with str(), any string value that parses as JSON comes back as a different type: set('123') returns 123, set('true') returns True, set('null') returns None. The round-trip through set/get no longer preserves the value's type.

There are no tests for the new persistence behaviour: data round-trip, the fallback for old rows with data=NULL, initial_tokens capped at bucket_size, and the denied path persisting refilled tokens. The committed checklist says tests were added, but the diff has none, and the PR template leaves 'added tests' unchecked. This is the regression the PR fixes, so it should be covered.

A personal working checklist was committed to the repo root. It contains the author's absolute local filesystem paths (/Users/<author>/...) and claims tests were added, which they weren't. Remove it from the change.

The changelog says 'apply the latest migration before upgrading', but the migration ships with the new version and can only run after upgrading. It should say to run `migrate` immediately after upgrading, and should mention the BigAutoField PK change and the index renames, which this migration also makes.

Run infrastructure setup before launching the compound. When launching the full-stack compound, VS Code starts its configurations concurrently, but infrastructure setup is only a prerequisite of the API configuration. Python can therefore bind port 5002 before setup runs `docker compose ... up -d`, which also starts the Docker exp container on port 5002. This causes setup to fail with a port conflict and prevents the API debugger from launching. Make infrastructure setup a compound-level prerequisite before launching any services. The root launch configuration has the same issue.

Use an authenticated or TCP-based Azurite health check. Azurite's account-level container-list operation requires authentication, so this unsigned request does not return a successful status even when storage is ready. Since `waitForHealth` only accepts `response.ok`, every local startup and debug setup waits the full 60-second timeout and reports a false readiness warning. Use a TCP probe, as the existing Compose health check does, or authenticate the storage request.

Validate bare-metal configuration before replacing Docker exp. On a fresh checkout, `sites/exp.arolariu.ro/config.json` does not exist, and neither setup nor this orchestrator creates it. The bare-metal loader consequently falls back to `config.template.json`, whose database connection strings are placeholders and whose API URL uses HTTPS while the new API profile serves HTTP. Thus the documented `npm run dev:local` workflow replaces Docker exp with configuration that cannot connect to the infrastructure it just started. Validate the required local configuration and provide an actionable setup step, or generate appropriate local defaults before switching services.

The `--setup-only` profile used by the VS Code `Infra: Setup Docker` preLaunchTask still runs `swapExpToBareMetalMode()`, which stops the Docker exp container, but it starts no bare-metal exp in its place. If you run `.NET API: Debug` on its own (root launch.json or the backend workspace), nothing is listening on :5002 and the API can't fetch its config. The only setup where this works is the compound config that also launches the Python exp. Either skip the exp stop in setup-only mode or make the API launch config depend on exp being up.

`main()` waits on `Promise.race` for any child to exit, then just returns with nothing logged and no exit code. If one service crashes (for example the API fails at startup), the orchestrator stays silent while the others keep running, and the crashed service's exit status is lost. It should report which service exited, pass on a non-zero code, and shut the siblings down or say clearly that they are still running.

Children are spawned with `shell: true`, so `p.kill()` only signals the intermediate shell. The `npx → nx → dotnet watch/uvicorn/next` grandchildren can be orphaned, especially on Windows or when the parent gets SIGTERM from VS Code task termination. They then keep holding ports 3000/5000/5002, which matches the 'Port already in use' problem listed in the troubleshooting table. Spawn without a shell, or kill the whole process tree or group.

`npm run generate` with no flags does nothing: `scripts/generate.ts` prints a 'use one or more flags' tip and returns. So the new `postStartCommand` doesn't 'auto-generate files' as the PR claims. Adding `/env` wouldn't fix it, because `generate.env.ts` prompts on stdin through readline and would hang a non-interactive postStart. On top of that, `2>/dev/null || true` hides every failure.

The docs say `npm run generate` will 'Generate all (env, i18n, GraphQL)', but without flags it generates nothing; you need e.g. `npm run generate /env /i18n /gql`. The same file (lines 144, 304) and `.env.example` line 11 also say `npm run generate:env` creates `.env` 'with sensible defaults'. In reality it prompts interactively for every missing key.

Every entry has a trailing `# comment` on the same line, and the file tells users to copy it to `.env`. The repo's own `.env` parser (`fetchConfigurationFromLocalEnvFile` in scripts/generate.env.ts) does not strip inline comments. That means `SITE_ENV=DEVELOPMENT   # "DEVELOPMENT" or "PRODUCTION"` keeps the comment as part of the value, and empty secrets like `CLERK_SECRET_KEY=   # Clerk secret key` become non-empty junk, so the generator won't even prompt for them. Put the comments on their own lines.

Setting `NODE_OPTIONS=--inspect` on an `npm run dev` launch makes the npm process itself take the inspector port 9229. The child (vite/next) then fails with 'address already in use', so the debugger lands on npm instead of the dev server. js-debug already auto-attaches to child processes for node launch configs, so the flag is unnecessary and breaks things. The website's `dev` script also passes `--inspect` already. The same pattern appears in fullstack.code-workspace (lines 95, 140), and in the compound config several Node targets fight over 9229.

Port 5002 can be claimed twice. `startStorage()` runs `docker compose up -d` on Storage, which also starts the Docker `exp` container on host port 5002, and only then does `swapExpToBareMetalMode()` stop it. If a bare-metal exp is already running, `up -d` cannot bind 5002, `dockerCompose` throws, and the whole setup aborts. This happens on a second `npm run dev:local`, or with the root/fullstack compound: there `Python: exp FastAPI` starts at the same time as `.NET API: Debug`'s preLaunchTask (`Infra: Setup Docker` → `--setup-only`). If Docker wins the race instead, uvicorn fails to bind. Fix: start only the storage services you need (`up -d mssql cosmosdb azurite redis`), or add a compose profile so `exp` is left out.

Children are spawned with `shell: true`, so `p.kill()` only signals the intermediate shell (or `cmd.exe`). The `nx` → `dotnet watch`/`uvicorn`/`next dev` grandchildren can be left orphaned and keep holding ports 3000/5000/5002, which breaks the next run. Also, when any one service exits (for example exp crashes because Python deps are missing), `Promise.race` resolves and `main` returns without saying anything while the other services keep running. Spawn without a shell, or kill the process tree (detached process group plus `process.kill(-pid)`, `taskkill /T` on Windows), and report or propagate the exit of the first child.

The devcontainer uses `docker-outside-of-docker`, so the compose containers run on the host daemon and their published ports are not reachable at `localhost` inside the devcontainer. That makes the documented DevContainer flow (`npm run dev:local` inside the container) fail: the health checks and Cosmos/Azurite init against `localhost:8081`/`10000` time out or fail, and the bare-metal API/website cannot reach the databases at the localhost URLs. DEVELOPMENT.md also wrongly says Docker-in-Docker is enabled. Either switch to `docker-in-docker` or document and handle the host-network difference.

Python 3.12 is added, but nothing installs `sites/exp.arolariu.ro/requirements.txt`. Use `charliermarsh.ruff` as the Python default formatter here, in fullstack.code-workspace, and in the devcontainer recommendations.

Preserve existing original values for tracked read-only properties. When an already tracked entity has a read-only property changed and is then passed to `context.Update(entity)`, this overwrites its legitimate original value with the changed value. Subsequent change detection no longer detects the forbidden modification, so `SaveChanges()` silently ignores it instead of throwing. For a read-only concurrency token, this also replaces the original value used for concurrency checks. Restrict the snapshot repair to the disconnected complex-discriminator scenario rather than resetting every property configured with `AfterSaveBehavior.Throw`.

This overwrites the original value of every property with AfterSaveBehavior.Throw, and primary key properties are always Throw. The block runs whenever an entry goes to Modified with modifyProperties, including Unchanged→Modified via `entry.State = Modified` and Modified→Modified via `Update()` on an already-tracked entity. In those cases the original value is real store state, not an unreliable default. Example: with AutoDetectChanges off, the user changes a key or a Throw-configured property on a tracked entity, then sets State = Modified. The real change is erased: the property is no longer detected as modified, SaveChanges no longer throws, and the update is built from the current values. For a key, the UPDATE's WHERE clause would use the new key value, so it could update a different row or fail with a concurrency error. Before this change, SaveChanges threw. The fix should be limited to the Detached→Modified case (where original values come from the snapshot factory) or to the affected shadow/complex discriminator properties.

This treats the symptom, not the root cause. After #37394, the snapshot factory stores default values for shadow properties on complex types, so the original discriminator value is wrong. The workaround only runs on the `newState == Modified && modifyProperties` path. Other paths keep the same bad snapshot: `Attach()` (Unchanged) followed by modifying a different property, or setting a single property as modified. On those paths DetectChanges still sees the discriminator (null) differ from the current value, marks it modified, and SaveChanges throws the same 'read-only after it has been saved' exception. A fix in the snapshot or original-value initialization, as #38111 apparently does, would cover every path.

The code comment marks this loop as a hot path. It now calls EnsureOriginalValues plus a boxed `this[property]` read and SetOriginalValue for every key property (and any other Throw property) each time an entity is Updated or set to Modified. That adds per-entity overhead to every bulk Update, even though only complex-type shadow discriminators need it.

The test only covers Detached→Modified through Update(). It does not cover Attach() followed by a property change, or a regression test that changing a key or Throw property on a tracked entity and then setting State = Modified still throws. Those cases would expose the gap and the over-broad fix described above. It also never asserts that the discriminator is not marked modified after Update().

This overwrites the original value of every AfterSaveBehavior.Throw property whenever an entry is set to Modified with modifyProperties. That includes `entry.State = Modified` and `Update()` on an entity that is already tracked. Suppose a user changes a Throw property (a property configured with SetAfterSaveBehavior(Throw), or an alternate key) on an Unchanged entity and then calls Update() or sets State = Modified. Before this change, DetectChanges flagged the edit and SaveChanges threw the intended 'read-only after it has been saved' error. Now the real database-backed original value is silently replaced: the illegal edit is never saved and never reported, OriginalValues/GetDatabaseValues comparisons give wrong results, and any Throw property that is also a concurrency token or key would send the wrong value in the UPDATE's WHERE condition. The fix needs to be limited to the case it is meant for: detached → Modified, and/or properties whose snapshot value is a placeholder default.

This works around the symptom instead of the root cause. According to the description, the regression comes from the #37394 snapshot factory storing default values for shadow properties on complex types. Other paths still read that bad snapshot. For example, Attach() (Unchanged) followed by DetectChanges should still find a false mismatch on the discriminator, mark it Modified and throw at SaveChanges, and OriginalValues still report null for the discriminator. The fix belongs in the snapshot creation (as #38111 apparently does), or the Attach path also needs fixing and a test.

This is a hot path (the code itself says 'do not use LINQ'). Every Update()/State=Modified now boxes and writes the original value of every Throw property, which includes all primary and alternate key properties, even when nothing is wrong. That adds per-entity overhead to a common bulk-update pattern just to fix a narrow complex-type discriminator case.

The test only covers the disconnected Update() case. It has no test that a real change to a Throw property on a tracked entity followed by Update()/State=Modified still throws, which is the behavior this change can break. It also has no Attach() test and does not check that the discriminator's IsModified is false and that its OriginalValue is correct after Update(). Without these, the regression risks above are unguarded.

This change makes `--_fs-base` untyped by switching its syntax from `<length>` to `*`. `--_fs-base` drives every `--fs-*` token in the design system, so this global change is out of scope for a Legend feature, and nothing in the diff needs it. With `*`, an invalid value such as `--_fs-base: large` is no longer rejected at parse time and does not fall back to the 1rem initial value. Instead, every `calc()` built from `--fs-*` becomes invalid, and font sizes break silently across all components. The property also stops being animatable or interpolable. Please revert it, or justify it and test it separately.

This is a breaking change for anyone using `Legend` directly. (1) `className` used to be applied to the `role="list"` flex row and now goes on a new outer wrapper, so consumer styles aimed at the list (for example `flex-wrap` or `justify-content`) stop working. (2) The default `justify-content: center` was removed and the root is now an `inline-flex` aligned to flex-start. Every standalone legend that used to be centered is now left-aligned unless the caller adds `alignSelf="center"`, which the PR only did for the built-in charts. The PR has no changeset or migration note even though it changes behavior visibly.

The visible label and the list's accessible name are the same string, so the visible label is applied as a duplicated `aria-label` and not linked with `aria-labelledby`. Screen readers read the heading text and then announce "list, Sales by product" again. It also breaks the link between the visible label and the name, which matters for translation and voice-control. Give the label an id (`useId`) and point to it with `aria-labelledby`. Separately, `label=""` hides the visible label (falsy check) but sets `aria-label=""` (`??` only checks for null or undefined), which leaves the list with no accessible name instead of falling back to "Chart legend".

Size variants use `[data-size]` attribute selectors. The package conventions (AGENTS.md) say: "Variants and sizes: use cva-generated classes, not data-attributes; data-attribute selectors for RAC state only." Generate a size class with `cva` instead. Also, `.root` sets `font-size: var(--fs-sm)` and the `md` variant sets the same value again, which is redundant.
`font-weight: bold` breaks the package rule: "Font-weight: use `bolder` when text needs bold... No numeric weights or `bold`." Use `bolder`.

The `useMemo` here adds complexity without measurable benefit. The `series` arrays in the examples, and likely in most callers, are new on every render, so the memo is recomputed every time anyway. Mapping a handful of items is cheap. Render the items inline.

These tests don't check the behavior they describe. `assume(locator).exists()` only checks that a Locator object exists, and Locators are always truthy whether or not anything matches, so the label test passes even if no list has the accessible name. The 'stacks items vertically' test only counts list items and never checks the vertical layout (for example, `flex-direction: column` or the items' y-positions). Use `await expect.element(...).toBeInTheDocument()` and assert on the layout.

The horizontal list doesn't wrap (no `flexWrap`), and the root is now an `inline-flex` box centered with `alignSelf`. In both charts the legend's parent has `overflow: hidden`, so if a chart has many series or long names, items that overflow the chart width are clipped. Readers lose series names with no visual sign that anything is missing. Since the PR's goal is to handle tight horizontal space, add `flexWrap="wrap"` for horizontal orientation.

Breaking visual change to the public `Legend` component. The root used to be a block-level flex row with `justify-content: center`. It is now `display: inline-flex` with `align-items: flex-start`, so any consumer that renders `<Legend>` on its own (outside BarChart/LineChart) will see the legend jump from centered to start-aligned. Only the built-in charts were patched with `alignSelf="center"`. Either keep centering as the default (for example, center the list inside a full-width root) or document this as a breaking change in the changeset/release notes.

This changes the global `@property --_fs-base` syntax from `<length>` to `*`. That is unrelated to the legend and affects every `--fs-*` token in the design system. It removes type validation, so invalid values are no longer rejected and replaced by the 1rem initial value. It also stops the value from being computed to an absolute length, so relative units now resolve wherever the token is used, and the property can no longer be interpolated or animated. The legend doesn't need this change. Nothing in the PR justifies it beyond 'broader compatibility', so it should be reverted or moved to its own reviewed change.

The visible label and the list's name are wired together by duplicating the string into `aria-label`, not by referencing the label element. The text isn't programmatically linked, and some screen readers will announce it twice (once as text, once as the list name). Give the label an id (`useId`) and use `aria-labelledby` on the list. Also, `label ?? 'Chart legend'` lets `label=""` produce an empty `aria-label`, which leaves the list unnamed. Use `label || 'Chart legend'` or check the trimmed value.

Size variants use `[data-size]` attribute selectors. The package conventions (AGENTS.md) say variants and sizes must use cva-generated classes, and that data-attribute selectors are reserved for RAC state. The `.root` base rule and the `[data-size="md"]` rule are also redundant, since both set `font-size: var(--fs-sm)`.
`font-weight: bold` breaks the documented project rule (variables.css and AGENTS.md): use `bolder` when text needs bold, and don't use `bold` or numeric weights.

The `useMemo` keyed on `series` adds overhead without benefit. Callers almost always pass a new array literal on each render (as every example does), so the memo never hits. Map the items inline as before.

`LegendProps` now spreads every remaining `FlexProps`, including `role`, `aria-label` and `aria-labelledby`, onto the outer wrapper and not onto the `role="list"` element. A consumer who passes `aria-label` to name the legend will label a generic div, while the list still announces as 'Chart legend'. Either omit these ARIA props or forward them to the list.

The new browser tests don't really check anything. `getByRole`/`getByText` return locator objects, so `assume(locator).exists()` passes even when nothing matches. They should use `await expect.element(...).toBeInTheDocument()` or similar. The 'stacks items vertically' test only counts list items and never checks the vertical layout (for example, `flex-direction: column` or item positions), so it would also pass for a horizontal legend.

Install the 32-bit MinGW toolchain before using it. The `windows-2025` hosted image does not provide a toolchain at `C:/mingw32`. Removing `msys2/setup-msys2` also removes the installation of the i686 compiler, and adding a directory to `PATH` does not install it. The x86_32 job now asks `godot-tools/windows.py` to invoke `C:/mingw32/bin/i686-w64-mingw32-g++`, so compilation fails and the dependent release job cannot run. Retain an explicit 32-bit toolchain installation and set `mingw_prefix` to its actual location.

The 'Setup MinGW path' step adds the hardcoded `C:/mingw32/bin` to PATH for both MinGW jobs. The x86_64 job therefore gets the 32-bit directory on PATH instead of `C:/mingw64/bin`. The added entry also comes before the image's default PATH, so if a 32-bit toolchain were ever present, its gcc/ar/windres would win any unprefixed tool lookup for the x86_64 build. The path should depend on the matrix entry, e.g. `C:/${{ matrix.msys }}/bin`.

The x86_32 MinGW job now relies on a GCC toolchain at `C:/mingw32` (via `mingw_prefix=C:/mingw32` and the PATH step). The windows-2025 runner image only ships a 64-bit MinGW-w64 at `C:/mingw64`, and since msys2/setup-msys2 was removed, nothing installs an i686 toolchain anymore. `godot-tools/windows.py` will then look for `C:/mingw32/bin/i686-w64-mingw32-gcc` (or the unprefixed `gcc`), so the job will fail or compile with the wrong toolchain. Add a step that downloads and installs an i686 MinGW (e.g. a WinLibs/niXman release) into `C:/mingw32`, or keep MSYS2 for the 32-bit build.

`mingw_prefix=C:/mingw64` makes `godot-tools/windows.py` build tool names as `C:/mingw64/bin/x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` etc. It is not confirmed that the preinstalled `C:/mingw64` toolchain on windows-2025 provides every target-prefixed binary SCons needs (including `ar`, `ranlib` and `windres`), or that its GCC version is new enough for this ANGLE revision (chromium/7219). Previously the job got a current GCC from MSYS2. Check the tool names in windows.py and pin or verify the GCC version, otherwise the build may break or quietly use an older compiler.

The `msys` and `msysenv` matrix keys are no longer used by any step now that msys2/setup-msys2 was removed. They are dead configuration and suggest MSYS2 is still involved, so remove them, or use `msys` to build the per-arch PATH.

The 'Setup MinGW path' step adds `C:/mingw32/bin` to PATH for every MinGW matrix entry, including the x86_64 job, whose `mingw_prefix` is `C:/mingw64`. The path should come from the matrix (for example a per-entry `mingw_prefix` value) so each job adds its own toolchain's bin directory. As written, the x86_64 job puts a 32-bit toolchain directory ahead of its own on PATH. If that directory exists, gcc's subprocesses (cc1plus, as, ld, lto plugins) can resolve or load the wrong-architecture binaries and DLLs (libgcc, libwinpthread, etc.). If it does not exist, the step does nothing useful.

The x86_32 job now assumes an i686 GCC toolchain at `C:/mingw32` on the stock `windows-2025` runner image. The image only ships a 64-bit MinGW-w64 at `C:\mingw64`, and nothing in the workflow installs a 32-bit one now that the MSYS2 setup (which installed `mingw-w64-i686-gcc`) was removed. `C:/mingw32/bin/i686-w64-mingw32-g++` will therefore not exist and the x86_32 GCC build will fail. Install an i686 toolchain explicitly, or keep MSYS2 for this entry.

This job now uses whatever MinGW-w64 build is preinstalled on the runner image instead of a pinned MSYS2 mingw64 package. The artifact is labeled 'MinGW/GCC (MSVCRT)', but nothing checks that the image's GCC targets MSVCRT rather than UCRT, or which threading/exception model it uses. The image toolchain can also change without notice when GitHub updates the image. Either of these can silently produce static libraries that are ABI-incompatible with consumers expecting MSVCRT-based GCC builds. Pin or verify the toolchain.
The `msys`/`msysenv` matrix keys are now dead because the msys2/setup-msys2 step was removed. They are misleading (they suggest MSYS2 is still used) and should be removed.

MinGW builds previously ran in an MSYS2 shell with `MINGW_PREFIX` set. They now run under default pwsh with `mingw_prefix` passed explicitly, which sends them through the 'cross-compilation' branch in godot-tools/windows.py instead of the native `mingw.generate` branch. Different tool definitions apply there (for example `gcc-ar`, and no `IMPLIBPREFIX`/`SHLIBSUFFIX` settings), so build output and flags may differ from earlier artifacts. Confirm this is intended.

Reserve preserved IDs before sanitizing older calls. When preservation is enabled, an older call such as `a_b` is sanitized to `ab` even if the latest assistant already has a preserved call named `ab`. Because preserved IDs never enter `used`, this introduces duplicate call IDs and ambiguous result associations in an otherwise distinct transcript. Reserve the latest turn's IDs before resolving historical IDs so collision handling can choose a different ID for the older call.

The latest assistant turn's tool-call ids are kept as-is, but they are never added to the `used` set that `makeUniqueToolId` checks to avoid collisions. An older id can therefore sanitize to the same value as a preserved one. Example: the latest call is `abc123` and an older call is `abc-123`, which becomes `abc123`. The request then contains two tool calls (and two tool results) with the same id, so the provider may reject it or pair results with the wrong call. This is the exact case the transcript-wide de-dup mapping exists to prevent. Fix: before the rewrite pass, add each preserved id to `used` and map it to itself, so older ids that collide with it get a suffix.

A tool result is left unchanged whenever its id is in `preservedLatestToolCallIds`, wherever it sits in the transcript. If an older assistant turn used the same raw id (some providers reuse ids like `call_0` or emit duplicates), that older turn's tool call gets rewritten but its matching result keeps the raw id. That leaves an orphaned result and an unpaired tool call, the very failure this change is meant to prevent. Only results that come after `latestAssistantIndex` should be preserved; earlier results should still go through `resolve`.

The new `preserveLatestAssistantTurn` option changes sanitization for a production provider, but the change adds no unit tests. The author also says nothing was run locally. There is no test showing that the latest assistant turn stays byte-identical, that its paired tool results are preserved while older ones are rewritten, or that the collision and older-turn cases above are handled. CI can't catch regressions in behavior it doesn't exercise. Add cases to the tool-call-id tests, like the existing `dropThinkingBlocks` preserve test in thinking.test.ts.

The latest assistant turn's tool-call ids are kept as they are, but they are never added to `used` (or to `map`). `makeUniqueToolId` therefore has no way to avoid them. An older id that sanitizes to the same string (for example older `call_1` becomes `call1` while the latest turn has `call1`, or two strict9 ids that truncate or hash to the same value) gets rewritten into a duplicate of a preserved id. The transcript then holds two tool_use blocks with the same id, and the older turn's tool result can be paired with the wrong call. Add the preserved ids to `used`, and map each one to itself, before the rewrite pass.

The skip check compares only the raw id against `preservedLatestToolCallIds` and ignores the result's position. If an older assistant turn used the same raw id as the latest turn (duplicated or replayed messages, retries, providers that reuse ids), that older tool call is rewritten through `resolve` but its tool result is left with the raw id. The older pair then no longer matches. This is the orphaned or mismatched tool-result failure the change is meant to prevent. Only skip tool results that come after `latestAssistantIndex`, or that belong to the latest turn's result block.

The latest assistant turn is skipped whenever the policy flag is set, without checking whether its ids are valid for the target. The flag depends only on the current provider/model (github-copilot + claude). If the latest assistant message came from another provider before a model switch (for example OpenAI Responses ids like `call_x|fc_y`, or ids that aren't alphanumeric), those raw ids are now sent to a strict-id endpoint with no sanitization. Consider preserving the turn only when its ids already pass `isValidCloudCodeAssistToolId`, or only when the message's provider/model matches the current one.

This code picks the latest assistant as any message with role `assistant`. `dropThinkingBlocks` in `thinking.ts` instead requires `Array.isArray(content)`. If the last assistant message has non-array or missing content, the two sanitizers preserve different messages. One then rewrites the turn the other treated as the protected latest turn. Share one helper so both pick the same message.

The flag only goes as far as tool-id sanitization. The rest of `sanitizeSessionMessagesImages` still rebuilds the latest assistant message: it always creates a new object, runs `sanitizeContentBlocksImages`, and in `full` mode also runs `stripThoughtSignatures` and drops empty text blocks. So the latest turn still isn't replayed verbatim in every case, even though the CodeRabbit release notes say image sanitization respects this policy. Either skip the latest assistant index here too, or correct the claim.

No tests cover the new `preserveLatestAssistantTurn` path: latest turn left unchanged, its tool results left unchanged, older turns still sanitized, no collisions with preserved ids. The author also says TypeScript and Vitest were not run locally. The existing tool-call-id tests should be extended, especially since this is a fix for a live provider rejection.

This change probably doesn't fix the staging failure. The old jq program's quoting was correct: tracing the local double quotes, the remote `sh` and then `bash -lc` hands jq exactly the intended filter, with `$cfg` and the other variables single-quoted. A quoting problem in a jq filter also shows up as a compile/syntax error. `parse error: Invalid numeric literal` is different: jq raises it when its *input* isn't valid JSON. That points to `.runtime-openclaw.json` itself, e.g. JSON5/comments, a partially written file or something non-JSON at the path. If so, `JSON.parse` fails on the same file with a SyntaxError and the step still fails, just with a different message. Before merging, confirm the file's real format on staging (the PR's own follow-up already suggests this). If the runtime config may be JSON5, parse it with the app's own JSON5 loader. At minimum, on parse failure print the error and the first bytes of the file so the next failure can be diagnosed.

The description says this follows the existing `browser_probe_js` pattern, but it doesn't. That probe uses a quoted heredoc plus `printf '%q'` and passes the script straight to `docker exec ... node -e`, with no inner `bash -lc` and no hand-escaped quotes. This one is a single minified line of JS inside three layers of shell quoting (`'\''` and `\"`). That is the same fragile style the PR says it is removing, and it is hard to review or edit safely. Move it into a `<<'NODE'` heredoc, escape it with `printf %q`, and call `docker exec ${container_escaped} node -e ${..._escaped}` directly, as Check 8 does.

This doesn't match the old validation exactly. `typeof cfg.credentialRoutes[route]==="object"` is also true for arrays, which jq's `type == "object"` rejected. If a route is accidentally configured as an array, the JS reads `active.mode` as undefined and exits 1 with no message, while every probe failure gives the same generic `Failed to inspect active Google Workspace credential route mode` error. Add `!Array.isArray(...)` and write a specific reason to stderr before `process.exit(1)` (route missing, route not an object, mode missing), so operators can tell a misconfiguration from a parse or SSH failure.

The probe still reads `/home/node/.openclaw/.runtime-openclaw.json` with plain `JSON.parse`. Nothing in the repo creates that file. The deployed config lives at `$OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` (see docker-compose.yml:26), and deploy.sh and the Check 8 probe both read it with `JSON5.parse` plus `$include` resolution. A jq error of 'Invalid numeric literal' usually means the input isn't strict JSON (JSONC/JSON5 comments, unquoted keys, trailing commas) or that the file is missing or different from what's expected. It doesn't point to a shell-quoting problem. `JSON.parse` rejects the same input, so this change most likely turns the jq parse error into a Node SyntaxError and staging verify still fails. Read `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` with JSON5 and the shared include resolver, the way `browser_probe_js` does, so the check sees the same config the gateway uses.

When `defaultCredentialRoute` is missing or null, the probe calls `process.exit(1)`, and verify then fails with 'Failed to inspect active Google Workspace credential route mode'. The plugin accepts that config: in legacy mode, config.ts:370-376 creates a default route when `credentialRoutes` is empty, and a null default with explicit bindings is also valid. The probe doesn't copy that logic, so valid deployments fail verify even though they should reach the 'skipping credentials file check' branch. The probe also doesn't `trim()` route names the way the plugin does. Either reproduce the plugin's resolution logic or print a non-failing `mode` so the skip path runs.

Every failure looks the same from the outside: a missing route or mode exits 1 with nothing on stderr, a parse error prints a stack trace that `gce_ssh_lastline` mostly hides, and verify only reports 'Failed to inspect active Google Workspace credential route mode'. The PR's follow-up plan relies on finding out the real runtime shape, so write a specific reason to stderr before exiting (missing file, parse failure, missing default route, missing mode) and make sure it shows up in CI logs.

The PR description says this follows the `browser_probe_js` pattern, but it doesn't. That probe keeps its JS in a quoted heredoc and passes it through `printf '%q'` with no extra `bash -lc` layer. This change embeds a long one-line script inside three levels of hand-escaped quoting (local double quotes, remote shell `'\''`, then `bash -lc`), which is the fragility the PR is trying to remove. Moving the JS into a heredoc and using `%q` like Check 8 would make it readable and safer to edit. The current version also uses `typeof ... === "object"`, which accepts arrays.

Size nodes with annotations even when compartments are absent. For a node with annotations but no compartments, the renderer now draws annotations above the title, but this condition bypasses class sizing. Consequently, annotation width and height are not reserved and the title remains centered in the original box, allowing annotations to overlap it or extend outside the node. Include annotation-only nodes in the sizing path.

Measure annotation height using its rendered lines and font size. When an annotation contains multiple lines or overrides `FontSize`, the renderer advances by its actual font size for every rendered line, whereas this calculation reserves only one title-sized line per annotation. The class title and first divider can therefore overlap the annotation. Calculate the reserved height from each annotation's rendered line count and effective font size.

Reserve and advance space for every compartment label line. For a compartment label containing newlines or a multiline `Label.Lines` value, the inner loop renders all lines, but `currentY` advances by only one line afterward. The next label or divider therefore overlaps the additional lines. `SizeClassNode` likewise allocates only one line per label, so fixing the rendering advance alone still leaves text outside the node; both calculations need to account for the rendered line count.

The annotation height in the header is `Annotations.Count * fontSize * lineHeight`, where `fontSize` is the class label's font size. The renderer draws every rendered line of each annotation and advances by `annFontSize * lineHeight` (SvgNodeWriter.cs:323-327). A multi-line annotation, or one with its own `FontSize`, therefore takes more vertical space than was reserved. It then overlaps the class name at `label:centerY` and can run past the header divider.

Each compartment `Label` gets exactly one line height, but a label may hold several lines (embedded `\n` or `Lines`). The width estimate already handles multi-line labels, so sizing is inconsistent. In the renderer (SvgNodeWriter.cs:353-359), every rendered line is drawn but `currentY` advances only one line height per `Label`. The extra lines overlap the next member and overflow the compartment and node bottom, which is the clipping this change is meant to fix.

Class sizing only runs when `Compartments.Count > 0`, but the renderer draws annotations whenever `Annotations.Count > 0` (SvgNodeWriter.cs:151). A stereotyped class with no members (e.g. `<<interface>> IFoo`) is sized as a standard node with no annotation space and no `label:centerY`. The annotation is then drawn at the top and the class name at `Height/2`, so they overlap or clip. Delegate to `SizeClassNode` when annotations are present too.

`PrepareNodeLabels` wraps only `node.Label` to `LayoutHints.MaxNodeWidth`. Annotation and compartment labels are never wrapped, but they now set the node width, so class nodes silently ignore `MaxNodeWidth`. Worse, the class name gets wrapped to the max width even when a long member line has already made the box wider, which leaves the header oddly wrapped inside a wide box.

The fallback header height used when `class:headerHeight` is missing ignores annotations and multi-line class names. It also applies `node.Label.FontSize ?? fontSize`, which is redundant because `fontSize` already resolves the label's font size. When the fallback is hit, dividers land on top of the class name or annotation text. Compute it the same way as the layout engine, or rely on the metadata only.

Dividers are drawn as straight lines from x=0 to `node.Width`, whatever the node's shape. Class nodes keep the default shape, a rounded rect with `theme.BorderRadius`. For a circle, diamond, pill or cloud, the dividers and left-aligned member text extend outside the outline. The layout engine also never forces a rectangular shape for compartment nodes. Force `Shape.Rectangle` for compartment nodes or clip the dividers to the shape.

Every test covers layout only; none covers the new SVG rendering (`AppendClassCompartments`). No test checks that dividers sit at `class:headerHeight`, that member text stays inside `node.Height`, or that annotations and the class name don't overlap. There are also no multi-line, custom-font-size or annotation-only cases, which is exactly where the layout and the renderer disagree.

The annotation band height is `Annotations.Count * fontSize * 1.15`. It uses the class-name font size and counts one line per annotation. The renderer (SvgNodeWriter.cs:318-327) moves down by `annFontSize * 1.15` for every rendered line of every annotation, and it places the first baseline using the label font size, not the annotation's. So if an annotation is multi-line or has a larger FontSize, the text runs past the reserved band and overlaps the class name, which sits at `label:centerY`. Sizing should add up the per-line height of each annotation with its own font size, the same way the renderer does.

Class sizing only runs when `Compartments.Count > 0`, but the renderer (SvgNodeWriter.cs:151) draws annotations whenever `Annotations.Count > 0`. A node with a stereotype and no compartments (e.g. `<<interface>> Foo` with no members) is sized as a standard node: there is no height for the annotation, and the label is vertically centred because `label:centerY` is never set. The annotation is then drawn at `pad + 0.85*fontSize`, on top of or next to the centred class name, and it can spill out of the box. The condition should also send annotation-only nodes to SizeClassNode.

A compartment Label can render as several lines (its `Lines` are set, or its text contains `\n`), and the inner loop draws each one while advancing `lineBaseline`. However, `currentY` only moves down by one line height per Label, so the next member is drawn over the extra lines. Sizing has the same flaw: DefaultLayoutEngine.cs:506-508 counts one line per Label, so the box is also too short and the text overflows past the bottom. Both places should use the rendered line count for each Label.

PrepareNodeLabels wraps only `node.Label` to `LayoutHints.MaxNodeWidth`. Annotation and compartment lines are measured unwrapped, and `node.Width` takes their maximum with no cap. A long member signature therefore makes class nodes ignore MaxNodeWidth, which is inconsistent with how every other node respects that hint.

ClassNode_Width_AnnotationContributesToWidth asserts `>=`. It would still pass if annotations were left out of the width calculation, because both nodes would have equal width. The test claims annotations affect width, so it should assert strictly greater (the annotation is much longer than the class name and the compartment line). More generally, no test checks that the renderer and the layout agree, e.g. that compartment text and annotations stay inside the header and the node's height. That gap is where the mismatches above sit.

Import the bivariate prefixes from their actual module. `./constants` exports neither `LAYER_BIVARIATE_PREFIX` nor `SOURCE_BIVARIATE_PREFIX`; both are defined in `~core/logical_layers/constants`. The shared style generator compares those thresholds against `linearNormalization` results. For example, an axis with steps spanning 0–100 now supplies values between 0 and 1 against those original thresholds, assigning hexagons to incorrect color classes. Preserve raw axis calculations or transform the thresholds consistently before delegating.

`LAYER_BIVARIATE_PREFIX` and `SOURCE_BIVARIATE_PREFIX` are imported from `./constants`, but they are not defined there. They live in `~core/logical_layers/constants`. Preserve unfilled circles for point legends. This deep-imports an internal build path (`@konturio/default-icons/tslib/figma-icons/Letter.js`). The test asserts the exact SVG path data (`M6 6H18V9.08508...`) from the third-party icon package. Any harmless icon redesign in a dependabot bump will fail this test. Assert on something stable instead, e.g. mock the icon or check that an svg is rendered with the expected color.

Only the no-fill branch is tested. No test checks that a circle (with the correct fill/stroke) still renders when `fill` or `circle-color` is provided, so a regression in the main path would go unnoticed.
